messages.subject: blavaan 0.4-8
messages.body_plain:
blavaan 0.4-8 is now on CRAN. It fixes a few bugs and updates how Stan model compilation is handled at installation. The plan is for this to be the final release of the 0.4 series, with the 0.5 series adding some multilevel functionality (initially, random intercepts for continuous observed variables).

Ed

messages.subject: Growth curve models on percentages
messages.body_plain:
Greetings all,

I would like to run a Bayesian growth curve model on manifest outcomes that are highly aggregated percentages (percentages at the country level). Data are not available at the individual level.   For the repeated outcomes, I would like to specify them as either uniform(a,b) or beta(shape, scale).  Is this possible?

Thanks in advance,

David

Blavaan is incredibly slow for me. I have implemented the suggestions. Are there any developments on this front?

Gabe

>  I very much care about the PPP ;-)

One solution for me/us might be to try listwise deletion in an initial phase of more complex projects, and then include the full sample in the final estimations. I will try that, given moderate missingness at around 5%. (I guess this approach will be more problematic with a higher proportion of missingness.)

> Christopher Bratt
> From: Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com>
> Sent: Saturday, February 18, 2023 12:55:59 AM
> To: christop...@gmail.com <christop...@gmail.com>; blavaan <bla...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
>
> Thanks, the main bottleneck is figuring out how to code the Stan model for maximal speed/efficiency. In the traditional case, you cycle through each row of the data and evaluate the model likelihood for each row. But if you have complete data, you can use the sample covariance matrix and sample mean in place of each row of the data (at least, you can do it for SEM). If you have complete data and don't care about the means, you can use the sample covariance matrix and Wishart distribution. This gives better speed for large datasets because you no longer have to do computations for each row of the data.
>
> And I might have already said it in a previous email, but if you don't care about the ppp (the model fit metric), then setting
>
> test = "none"
>
> should speed up some more.
>
> Ed
>

slp =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3 ...

How would I set the string priors to specify the distribution of the y's?

David

messages.subject: Re: Growth curve models on percentages
messages.body_plain:
David

As y's are the outcome variables, you cant set a prior on them specifically, because their means are based on the predictions of the model on their means.

Based on the growth model, the item intercepts will be fixed to 0 to identify the factors. So, the means have to be defined at the means of the latent factors. So, if the scores are around 0 and .3, you could set the factor means as

int ~ prior("normal(0.1, 0.2)")*1
 slp ~ prior("normal(0, 0.2)")*1

This will not fully truncate it (dont recommend it), but will define the expected means. You can do a quick visualization with the rnorm function, to see what fits your expectation

hist(rnorm(10000, .2, .2))

messages.subject: Common Method Variance in Psychometrics
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I couldnt find any information on the group and internet regarding this issue. Sorry if I'm doubling it right now.

My question is,  in social sciences- psychometrics there is a threat of Common Method Variance (CMV) -therefore bias- if we're using a survey from the same response method. In SEM studies from Classical Test Theory, there are some procedural and statistical remedies regarding CMV. For example Harman's single factor test, marker variable method, measured or unmeasured latent method are few of them. These could be applied to check if we're under threat of CMV.

Could we or should we also apply these in a Bayesian SEM ? If so how they should be reported ? are there any sources regarding this issue. Thats my point..

for a detailed view:

**Understanding and managing the threat of common method bias: Detection, prevention and control (Kock et al, 2021)

**Common method biases in behavioral research: A critical review of the literature and recommended remedies (Podsakoff et al, 2003)

messages.subject: Re: Common Method Variance in Psychometrics
messages.body_plain:
I think that CMV would be a problem for Bayesian SEM whenever it is a problem for frequentist SEM. I am not completely familiar with all the procedures that you mention, and I don't immediately know of Bayesian applications to CMV. But the procedures seem to involve model comparisons, and it would be possible to use a Bayesian metric like LOO or WAIC to do the comparison of Bayesian models.

Ed
